n: When Jehu kills her son Ahaziah, Athaliah—Ahab and Jezebel’s daughter—seizes Judah’s throne by murdering the royal heirs, her own grandchildren. David’s line, through which the Messiah was promised, nearly ends here.

f.g: the royal family; all potential heirs.

n: Ahaziah’s sister Jehosheba rescues baby Joash and hides him with his nurse in a bedroom. Chronicles adds that she was the wife of Jehoiada the high priest. One brave woman preserves the covenant line.

f.g: ‘Jehovah is an oath’; called Jehoshabeath in Chronicles.
a storeroom for bedding, used as a hiding place.

n: Joash is hidden in the temple for six years while Athaliah rules—the only queen to reign alone over Judah or Israel.
In the seventh year, the priest Jehoiada makes a secret pact with the military commanders, including the Carites (royal bodyguard), and shows them the hidden prince.

f.g: military officers commanding units of one hundred.

n: Jehoiada plans the coup around the Sabbath shift change, when guards come and go and extra troops can gather without suspicion.
Other units are posted at key gates to secure the palace.

f.g: an unknown gate, called the ‘Foundation Gate’ in 2 Chronicles 23:5.

n: The two units going off duty will stay to guard the young king at the temple.
The guards are to surround the king with weapons drawn and kill anyone who breaks through the ranks.
The commanders follow Jehoiada’s plan exactly, gathering both shifts.
Jehoiada arms them with David’s own spears and shields stored in the temple—a symbolic link to the founder of the dynasty.
The guards form a protective wall around the king from one side of the temple to the other.
Jehoiada brings out the boy, crowns him, gives him “the testimony,” and anoints him. The people clap and shout, “Long live the king!”

f.g: probably a copy of the covenant law, which the king was to keep.

n: Athaliah hears the noise and hurries into the temple courts.
She sees the boy king standing by the pillar where kings traditionally stood, surrounded by leaders and rejoicing crowds. She tears her clothes and cries, “Treason!”—ironic from a usurper.

f.g: possibly one of the two bronze pillars, Jachin and Boaz.

n: Jehoiada orders her taken out between the ranks, with anyone following her to be killed—but not in the sacred temple.
She is executed at the horse entrance to the palace.
Jehoiada leads a covenant renewal: the king and people pledge to be the Lord’s people, and the king and people also covenant with each other. True reform begins with covenant.
The people destroy Judah’s temple of Baal, smash its altars and images, and kill Baal’s priest Mattan. Guards are appointed over the Lord’s house.

f.g: a Baal temple in Jerusalem, likely built under Athaliah.

n: A grand procession escorts the king from the temple to the palace, where he takes the throne of his fathers.
The people rejoice and the city is at peace. The narrator notes again that Athaliah had been executed.
Joash (Jehoash) was just seven when he became king. His faithful guardian Jehoiada will guide his early reign.

f.g: a longer form of Joash: ‘Jehovah has given.’
